prompt.context: You are riding up a chairlift at a small ski resort in West Virginia with a fellow classmate. It's a great spring skiing day and probably one of the last weekends the resort is open for the year. Your friend had heard a rumor that the resort might be up for sale.
prompt.question: Your friend asks you how much you think the ski resort might be worth. How might you go about determining the value of the resort?

clarifying_info.a: Revenue comes from ticket sales and food purchased on site.

clarifying_info.q: When is the resort open / what are the operating hours?
clarifying_info.a: The ski resort is open Thursday–Sunday from December 1 to April 30 (winter season). In the summer it is used by a private Summer Camp that pays $500,000 for full access.

clarifying_info.q: How many staff does the resort have?
clarifying_info.a: There are 20 staff at the resort.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual growth rate?

exhibits.title: Ski Resort Prices and Attendance
exhibits.shows: A table showing ticket prices and average daily attendance broken down by season (Off Season: December and April; Peak Season: January to March) and by day type (Weekend vs. Weekday), with separate columns for Adult and Child tickets. Attendance for child tickets is expressed as a fraction of the adult figure.

off_season_weekday.adult_attendance: 1/3rd the number of adult weekend skiers

peak_season_weekday.adult_attendance: 3/4ths the number of adult weekend skiers

framework: Structure valuation as Present Value of future cash flows (DCF / growing perpetuity)
Estimate annual Revenue: ski ticket sales (off-season vs. peak, weekend vs. weekday, adult vs. child) + food/on-site spending + any off-season revenue
Estimate annual Costs: fixed costs (land lease, lift machinery, insurance, maintenance, staff) + variable costs (food COGS)
Calculate pre-tax profit = Revenue – Costs, then apply tax rate to get after-tax cash flow
Apply growing perpetuity formula: Value = CF / (r – g) using discount rate and growth rate
Sense-check the result and discuss key risks / value drivers

questions.prompt: Question 1: How would you measure revenue for the ski resort?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify multiple revenue streams: (1) ticket sales segmented by season and customer type, (2) food and beverage on-site, (3) other services such as lessons, parking, retail. Watch for realistic assumptions and logical progression through categories.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What might drive variation in these revenue numbers?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: snow conditions, weather, quality of food/lessons, presence of competing ski or winter-outdoor entertainment in the area, and the macro economy.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Exhibit 1): Calculate total ski-season ticket and food revenue.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through Exhibit 1 systematically—compute daily revenue per segment, scale to weekly, then multiply by weeks in each season (8 off-season, 12 peak). Add food spend ($8 per skier). Candidate should also recognise that this covers only Dec–April and ask about other revenue sources.

math.setup: Off Season: 8 weeks, Thurs–Sun (4 days/week). Peak Season: 12 weeks, Thurs–Sun. Skiers spend $8 on food on average. Calculate daily revenue per cell (price × attendance), aggregate to weekly, then to seasonal totals.
steps: Weekly off-season revenue: ($75,000+$21,000+$22,500+$6,000) × not double-counted — weekend 2 days + weekday 2 days: weekend days = ($75,000+$21,000)×2=$192,000; weekday days = ($22,500+$6,000)×2=$57,000; weekly total = $249,000 → casebook uses simplified totals: Total Weekly Off Season = $150,000+$42,000+$45,000+$12,000 = $249,000 (per week, 4-day week)

Total skiers: off-season weekly (1,500+600+500+200)×8=22,400 + peak weekly (2,000+800+1,500+600)×12=58,800 ÷ — total 92,800 — wait: weekly off=(1,500+600+500+200)×4days=11,200 skiers/week×8=... casebook states 92,800 total skiers
Food revenue: 92,800 × $8 = $985,600 (≈ round to $1,000,000 for ease)

questions.prompt: Question 4: Estimate costs and calculate after-tax cash flow.
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish fixed from variable costs. Fixed: land lease, chairlift machinery, insurance, general maintenance, employee wages. Variable: food COGS. Strong candidate will ask about or flag the tax shield before arriving at after-tax cash flow.

math.setup: Variable costs = 50% of food revenue (round food revenue to $1,000,000). Fixed costs = $500,000/month × 12 months = $6,000,000 (note: only open Dec–Apr but costs given as annual). Total costs = $6,500,000. Pre-tax profit = Revenue – Costs. After-tax CF = Pre-tax profit × (1 – tax rate).

questions.prompt: Question 5: How do you perform the valuation? Calculate the value of the resort.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognise that future cash flows need to be discounted. The appropriate model is a growing perpetuity (Gordon Growth Model): Value = CF / (r – g). Discount rate r = 14%, growth rate g = 4%.

math.setup: Growing perpetuity formula: Value = CF₁ / (r – g). CF = $2,310,000, r = 0.14, g = 0.04.
math.answer: Estimated value of the ski resort ≈ $23,100,000

brainstorming.prompt: What factors might cause variation in the ski resort's revenue?

categories.name: Weather & Conditions
ideas: Temperature and length of ski season

categories.name: Competitive Landscape
ideas: Presence of other ski resorts in the region

categories.name: Operational Quality
ideas: Quality and variety of food/beverage offerings
Availability and quality of ski lessons

categories.name: Macro & Demand Factors
ideas: Overall macro economy and consumer discretionary spending
Demographic trends (aging population, youth participation in skiing)
Travel and lodging costs in the region

categories.name: Pricing & Capacity
ideas: Season pass vs. day ticket mix
Special events or competitions hosted at resort

recommendation: The ski resort can be valued at approximately $23.1 million using a growing perpetuity model, based on estimated annual after-tax cash flows of ~$2.31 million, a discount rate of 14%, and a long-run growth rate of 4%.
risks: Revenue is highly dependent on weather and snow conditions, which are outside management's control
Fixed cost base of $6 million annually creates significant operating leverage—a bad snow season could rapidly erode profitability
Growth rate assumption of 4% may be optimistic given climate trends affecting ski seasons
The summer camp arrangement ($500K/year) could be renegotiated or cancelled, reducing base revenues
Single-location concentration risk in West Virginia
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on historical revenue and cost data to validate assumptions
Assess capital expenditure needs (lift upgrades, snowmaking equipment) not captured in the operating cost model
Evaluate land ownership vs. leasing structure and any environmental permits
Benchmark comparable ski resort transactions to triangulate valuation
Explore revenue enhancement opportunities (summer zip-lining, mountain biking, expanded F&B)
